lowConfidence.claim: rosetta: Apple silicon provides x86-style TSO ordering for Rosetta 2 translated code
lowConfidence.reason: Widely reported and stated on Wikipedia ('support of x86-64 memory ordering in the M1 SoC') but not documented by Apple; definition worded generally.
Era boundaries are approximate (introduced 2007, displaced by DDR4 from 2014); hedged with 'around'.

gaps: A hardware-specific saturation-core count and a definitive catalogue of MISD products: comparable measurements and a consistent stream-level classification were not reliably established here.

Rosetta performance attribution and a version-independent Linux spinlock instruction catalogue: the exact implementation contracts and representative measurements were not reliably established; model-level ordering is taught instead.

A product-by-product SIMD release history, generic speedup ranges and claims about which vector length most products use: reliable coverage of those hardware and benchmark specifics was not established in this review.

A complete A100/H100 and AMD configuration catalogue, generic launch/latency timings and universal throughput ratios: those version- and workload-specific values were not comprehensively verified here; the retained arithmetic examples state their hypothetical assumptions.

Generic picojoule ratios, FPGA clock/build/financial-market latency ranges, ASIC dollar/lead-time estimates and a cross-generation accelerator catalogue: comparable primary evidence for those design-specific claims was not reliably established; they are not needed for the retained mechanism and arithmetic examples.

A universal perf sampling default, PMU overhead figure and CPU miss-buffer count: these depend on tool version, permissions, processor and workload and were not reliably established for a single stated target.
